scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user provided a detailed situation where a British man moved to the US for work and is struggling to fit in because of cultural differences in humor and personality. He feels that his way of being, which is more direct and includes dark jokes, doesn't align with the more polite and "woke" culture in the US. He's been told by some colleagues that he's an AH (a-hole) and doesn't fit in, but his flatmates and a few colleagues like him. He's considering whether he's an AH for just being himself.

First, I need to understand what the action is. The action here is the man continuing to be himself despite the cultural differences and the negative feedback he's receiving. The question is whether this action is morally acceptable.

I think about morality in terms of whether the action respects others, causes harm, or violates any ethical principles. The man is trying to stay true to himself, which is generally seen as a positive trait. However, his behavior is causing friction with some of his colleagues, leading them to label him as an AH. 

I should consider the context. In the UK, his style of humor and communication is normal and accepted. In the US, the culture is different, and what he perceives as being himself might be seen as offensive or inconsiderate by others. He's made an effort to tone down his behavior when he realized it was causing issues, which shows he's trying to adapt. But even after toning down, some people still find his personality off-putting.

Is it morally wrong to stay true to oneself in a new environment? I don't think so. People have the right to express their personality as long as it doesn't harm others. However, the line can be blurry. If his behavior is causing others discomfort or making them feel disrespected, then it might be crossing into morally unacceptable territory.

He mentions that he's lost it at a colleague, which could imply he reacted negatively or aggressively. If that's the case, then losing his temper could be seen as morally unacceptable because it's a form of aggression. But the scenario doesn't provide specifics on how he lost it, so it's hard to judge.

Another angle is the concept of cultural adaptation. When moving to a new country, it's common to adjust one's behavior to fit in and show respect for the local customs. The man has made some adjustments, but he's struggling to fit in completely. It's a balance between staying true to oneself and respecting the host culture.

I also think about the impact on his work and relationships. If his personality is causing him to lose potential friends and colleagues, it might affect his career and well-being. However, he's still performing well in his job and has some supportive colleagues, so the impact might be limited.

In summary, the action of staying true to oneself isn't inherently morally wrong. However, the way he expresses himself might be causing harm or discomfort to others, which could make it morally questionable. Additionally, if his reaction to feedback involved aggression, that would be a separate issue.

I'm leaning towards the action being morally acceptable because he's not intentionally causing harm, but there's room for improvement in how he navigates cultural differences and communicates with others.
